name: Grooming routine (nails, ear/nose hair)

lead: A grooming routine covering nails and ear and nose hair is basic upkeep that makes you look neater and more polished up close. Clean, trimmed nails and tidy hair in the ears and nose remove small details that can otherwise read as unkempt.

The change is visible right after grooming. Trimming nails is listed among standard hygiene practices, and grooming is distinguished from hygiene as the part that supports a good appearance. No study has tested these habits against attractiveness ratings.

paras: People fold it into a regular routine: trimming and cleaning fingernails and toenails, and trimming ear and nose hair with a small trimmer or scissors. It is usually done alongside shaving, haircuts and skin care, and the results are immediate.
Risk is low. Sources describe no specific harms; as with any trimming tool, small nicks are possible, so careful use around the nose and ears is sensible.

angle.text: Tidy nails and trimmed ear and nose hair raise perceived polish, and the change shows right after grooming. Appearance communities treat it as basic upkeep that makes the whole look cleaner and more put-together.

lead: A grooming routine for nails and ear and nose hair is a set of basic upkeep habits: trimming and filing fingernails and toenails, and trimming stray hair that shows from the nostrils and ears. People do it to look neat and put-together in close-up settings such as conversation, handshakes and photos, where overgrown nails or visible nostril and ear hair stand out.[1][2][3]

Wikipedia lists trimming fingernails and toenails among generally accepted hygiene practices, and distinguishes grooming such as shaving or combing, which supports a good appearance, from hygiene itself.[1] Nails grow about 3.5 mm a month on the fingers and 1.6 mm on the toes, so regular trimming is part of upkeep, and filing smooths rough edges that can snag.[3] Nose and ear hairs tend to become longer, coarser and more noticeable with age.[4]

Guidance from health sources favours trimming over plucking for nose hair: rounded-tip scissors or an electric trimmer are described as the safest options, while plucking is associated with ingrown hairs and infections.[4] No published study tests nail or ear and nose hair care for effects on rated attractiveness.

paras: Personal hygiene is the set of practices that keep the body clean and healthy, motivated by reducing illness, well-being, social acceptance and avoiding passing illness to others.[1] Standards vary across cultures and change over time.[1] Grooming is described as the practice of cleaning and maintaining parts of the body.[2]

The best way to care for nails is described as trimming them regularly, with filing to smooth rough edges and small ridges.[3] Nails can dry out, peel, break or become infected, and tools shared between people can spread infection.[3] In a manicure the cuticle, the non-living part, is removed, but the living tissue at the nail base should not be touched because of the risk of pain, bleeding and infection.[3]

Nail changes can also reflect other conditions, including discolouration, ridges, brittleness and low levels of nutrients such as vitamin B12, iron or biotin, and persistent nail disease is described as something for a dermatologist to evaluate.[3]

Nose hairs filter dust, pollen and allergens before they reach the lungs.[4] Removal is a personal choice, and one health source states there is no health benefit to removing nose hair.[4] Trimming with rounded-tip scissors or an electric trimmer is described as the safest approach.[4]

Plucking is associated with ingrown hairs, nasal vestibulitis (a staph infection) and, rarely, deeper follicle infections; a 2011 study of 233 people with seasonal allergies found that those with the least nose hair had a higher asthma risk.[4] Laser removal is an alternative but costs more and carries risks.[4]
Wikipedia notes a 2007 study by Nelson and Geher in which people who chose their romantic partner reported more mutual grooming, linked to relationship satisfaction and trust.[2]
No studies found of nail or ear and nose hair care for appearance outcomes. A 2011 study of people with seasonal allergies reported by Healthline looked at nose hair amount and asthma risk.[4]
